doc.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Joe Williams's impact, Dr. Jive, and acting ability
summary: Every Day crossed over to R&B radio, which Gitler monitored for Prestige; he also praises Williams as an actor, from Newport with Cannonball to Cosby Show.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: that really helped establish that band because the R & B shows, the D.J.s were playing Basie and the young kids started to listen to this band. It wasn’t played just on jazz shows, because of some of the things they did. And I remember because I was working for Prestige Records at the time and we had to monitor Tommy “Dr. Jive” Smalls. He was the D.J. on WWRL out in Long Island. And they were slipping him five or ten dollars to play some of the Prestige numbers, right? So we had to, while we were packing boxes and stuff, we had to listen to see if he was playing it. Well naturally you heard everything else: B.B. King doing the “Three O’clock Blues” and Count Basie with Joe Williams doing “Every Day.” And so that really helped put that band over. He was a very important part of that band. And of course continuing on with a number of things he did that were all big, “The Comeback” and a lot of different things. And then of course he branched out and I started to see him in another light, his ability as an actor. And of course that helps him to this day to present his songs, because he really puts a lot of other ingredients into it than just singing. He’s definitely an actor. And when I saw him on stage at the Newport Jazz Festival in New York, I guess this was in the early seventies when it came from Newport and settled in New York, Cannonball Adderley and Joe combine on a thing, it was like the legend of John Henry. I think it was called “Big Man” if I’m not mistaken. And Joe’s ability as an actor that I had always seen really came to the fore. And I’m surprised that nobody ever took advantage of putting him in a musical, because he could have carried this off grandly, both as an actor and as a singer. You know I used to think this about Sarah Vaughan. I don’t know if she could have handled the acting, but I would have loved to have heard her in a Broadway musical just to hear her singing on stage in a certain setting. But he definitely could have done it. And of course later he shows up on the Cosby Show as the grandfather, and you know he’s marvelous. He’s got humor, he’s got pathos, he’s got all the attributes that an actor has to have. And whenever you see him in performance, these things come out and he puts those songs over, he gets to the audience, you know, just in an ungimmicked way. Because it’s all, again, getting back to Dizzy and Louis Armstrong, it’s all part of the persona. It’s all one thing. It’s not just this is sticking out and saying oh boy, he’s doing this.
